newsitem.title: PERU: Peru hostages' fate on line as rebel chief talks.
newsitem.headline: Peru hostages' fate on line as rebel chief talks.

text.p: The fate of 72 VIP hostages in Peru was finally on the bargaining table after the Marxist rebel leader sat down face-to-face with government officials for the first time in the 66-day-old crisis.

After three sets of talks-about-talks last week between officials and the rebel No. 2, Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini met government negotiator Domingo Palermo for 3-1/2 hours in a safe house on Friday.
It was the first time Cerpa had left the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence since his squad of rebels interrupted a diplomatic cocktail party to seize the building on Dec. 17.

Roman Catholic Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani, one of three guarantors overseeing negotiations, read out a statement to reporters that the talks were carried out in "a constructive atmosphere" and had gone to the heart of the matter.

"We have started to deal with various important issues which require an in-depth analysis," he said. In keeping with the pact of silence by all sides on the precise content of the meetings, Cipriani did not give more details but announced the next talks would be held on Monday.
Cerpa was driven to the meeting in a Red Cross car accompanied by his deputy Rolly Rojas, alias "The Arab."
As the car covered the short distance from the diplomatic compound, the MRTA rebels sang a revolutionary anthem commemorating fallen comrades and shouted defiant slogans.
"On the 65th day of the takeover of the residence, no one gives up, damn it," the rebels shouted in unison.
"What is the objective of this mission?" shouted a rebel through a megaphone. "To free our prisoners," replied others.

The 15-odd MRTA rebels' demand for the release of some 400 jailed comrades has been a bitter sticking point with the government. President Alberto Fujimori insists he will not consider this demand, although he is prepared to let the hostage-takers seek asylum abroad.

But a top congressmen, asked about a possible amnesty for MRTA prisoners, did not rule it out. "Congress is prepared to study the proposals made by the government," deputy speaker Carlos Torres Torres Lara told reporters, although he stressed that so far no such proposal exists.
The renewal of direct contact last week after a long period of deadlock and mutual insults prompted speculation the MRTA might modify its position on the prisoners issue.

In an interview with Reuters at a secret jungle location in eastern Peru this week, the MRTA admitted publicly for the first time it probably would not win its central demand that all jailed comrades be freed.

"I do not think all of the 400-plus (prisoners) are going to get out," said a man who identified himself as Comrade Alejandro, a member of the MRTA's top policy-making body. He said the MRTA was prepared to negotiate how many would be freed depending on their experience and importance in the movement.
The jungle commander also doubted Cerpa would ever drop completely the demand for the release of jailed rebels.

Also present at Thursday's talks were the two other guarantors -- Red Cross representative Michel Minnig and Canadian ambassador Anthony Vincent. The Japanese government's observer Terusuke Terada also attended.
A metal detector was used to make sure nobody entered the Red Cross-supervised safe house with weapons.

The MRTA stormed the residence on Dec. 17, initially taking more than 500 cocktail party guests hostage. But it released most in the early days of the crisis, holding only those it considered most valuable.

The remaining captives, many middle-aged and now ailing, include Fujimori's younger brother, two government ministers, top security force and judicial officials, two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats, and the ambassadors of Japan and Bolivia.

The rebels insisted on Thursday that no more hostages could be freed on medical grounds, claiming that they could get adequate treatment inside the residence. "Any illness is the product of negotiations dragging on," a statement issued over the Internet on behalf of the MRTA's high command said.
Some of the hostages require close monitoring for cancer, heart problems and arthritis. The last two released were freed due to poor health in January.
